source: KDT8 ch56, ch57, ch60-63; Katzung16 appendix 2; Sarkar p576-580

cards.front: Outline the evolution of India's tuberculosis control programme.
cards.back: Treatment of TB in India is free for all patients under a national programme. The Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP) began in 1997 and revised its treatment guidelines several times, most recently (in KDT) in 2016. TB became a notifiable disease in 2012, so every treating doctor must notify cases. After WHO's End TB Strategy, RNTCP was renamed the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP).

cards.front: What is DOTS, and what principles of short-course chemotherapy underlie it?
cards.back: Directly observed treatment, short course, recommended by WHO in 1995, used 6-8 month multidrug regimens with weight-based standard doses. All first-line drugs are given as a single daily dose; an intensive phase of 4-6 drugs rapidly kills bacilli and converts sputum, and a continuation phase of 3-4 drugs removes the remaining bacilli to prevent relapse. Directly observed treatment remains NTEP's patient-friendly way of monitoring adherence.

cards.front: Which drugs make up the NTEP intensive phase for new drug-sensitive TB, and for how long?
cards.back: Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for about 2 months (eight weeks).
refs: WEB NTEP Chapter 4 Treatment of Tuberculosis https://ntep.in/node/507

cards.front: Which drugs make up the NTEP continuation phase for new drug-sensitive TB, and what is the total duration?
cards.back: Isoniazid and rifampicin, with ethambutol added as the third drug for all new cases. Total treatment is 6 months.
refs: WEB NTEP Chapter 4 Treatment of Tuberculosis https://ntep.in/node/507

cards.front: What happened to the NTEP standard retreatment regimen formerly called Category II?
cards.back: It has been withdrawn from NTEP.
refs: WEB NTEP Chapter 4 Treatment of Tuberculosis https://ntep.in/node/507

cards.front: In what dosage form is the NTEP drug-sensitive regimen supplied?
cards.back: Fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets.
refs: WEB NTEP Chapter 4 Treatment of Tuberculosis https://ntep.in/node/507

cards.front: How did the RNTCP 2016 regimen for new drug-sensitive TB differ from the 2010 regimen, and why?
cards.back: The 2016 regimen is 2HRZE followed by 4HRE (6 months). Ethambutol was added to the continuation phase (2010 used RH only), as WHO advises where primary isoniazid resistance is common (up to 18%). Dosing was changed from thrice weekly to daily in both phases, because thrice-weekly dosing had been an operational compromise.

cards.front: Why does the TB programme use fixed-dose combination tablets in weight bands?
cards.back: FDCs make sure the patient takes all the drugs together, so bacilli are never exposed to only one or two drugs and resistance is not fostered. For operational ease the programme supplies separate FDC tablets for the intensive and continuation phases, with the number of tablets set by body-weight band.

cards.front: How did the TB programme extend to drug-resistant TB?
cards.back: RNTCP began DOTS-Plus in 2000 for diagnosis and treatment of MDR-TB, updated it in 2010 per WHO, and revised it again in 2016 with extensive drug-susceptibility testing: liquid culture DST, line probe assay (R and H resistance) and cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT, R resistance). A standard MDR regimen is used unless DST or patient factors call for an individualised regimen.

cards.front: Has the NTEP drug-sensitive regimen changed since the 2016 RNTCP regimen (2HRZE/4HRE)?
cards.back: The NTEP chapter gives the same shape: about 2 months of four drugs, then isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol, 6 months in all. The change to note is the withdrawal of the Category II retreatment regimen (next card).
refs: WEB NTEP Chapter 4 Treatment of Tuberculosis https://ntep.in/node/507

cards.front: How long is the NTEP continuation phase in neuro and spinal TB?
cards.back: Extended to 10 months.
refs: WEB NTEP Chapter 4 Treatment of Tuberculosis https://ntep.in/node/507

cards.front: Trace the history of leprosy control in India.
cards.back: The National Leprosy Control Programme began in 1955 and became the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) in 1982. Following the WHO Action Programme, multidrug therapy (introduced by WHO in 1981) was implemented through NLEP in 1982. India reached elimination as a public health problem (prevalence below 1 per 10,000) in December 2005, although some states remain above that level.

cards.front: What is the aim of MDT in a mass programme, and how does it differ from institutional care?
cards.back: Mass programmes (WHO Action Programme, NLEP) aim to make patients non-contagious and cut transmission, so fixed-duration therapy (12 months for multibacillary, 6 months for paucibacillary) is accepted; the few relapses are retreated with the same MDT, since persisters stay drug-sensitive. Private or institutional care aims to cure each patient and may continue up to about 4 years in highly bacillated cases.

cards.front: What has MDT achieved in India, as recorded in KDT?
cards.back: Prevalence fell from 57.6 per 10,000 in 1981 to 0.66 per 10,000 in 2016; total cases fell from 3.95 million (1981) to about 0.127 million new cases detected in 2015-16. Relapses were few, and lepra reactions did not become more common with MDT. India still has the largest number of leprosy patients in the world.

cards.front: How does NLEP (2009) classify leprosy for treatment, and why simplify it?
cards.back: Paucibacillary (PBL): 1-5 skin lesions, no nerve or only one nerve involved, skin smear negative at all sites. Multibacillary (MBL): 6 or more lesions, more than one nerve involved, or smear positive at any site. Two operational groups let field workers choose the regimen without lab skills; MBL patients are infectious, PBL are not.

cards.front: Which drugs make up leprosy MDT, and why three drugs instead of dapsone alone?
cards.back: Rifampin + dapsone + clofazimine (clofazimine omitted in PBL). Dapsone monotherapy led to resistance (first noted 1964) and relapse in up to 20%; MDT covers resistant strains, prevents new resistance, shortens treatment and kills persisters.

cards.front: Complete: NLEP MDT regimen
cards.text: MBL gets rifampin {{600 mg}} once monthly supervised, dapsone {{100 mg}} daily, and clofazimine {{300 mg}} monthly plus {{50 mg}} daily, for {{12 months}}. PBL gets rifampin and dapsone only, for {{6 months}}.

cards.front: What does the National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027 aim for?
cards.back: A leprosy-free India with zero infection and disease, zero disability, and zero stigma and discrimination. Strategies: stronger leadership and partnerships, early case detection, quality services, prevention of disease, disability and discrimination, and digital surveillance of individual patient records (Nikusth 2.0). The Sparsh Leprosy Awareness Campaign targets stigma.

cards.front: Why can rifampin be given once a month in MDT, and when must it be withheld?
cards.back: Rifampin is strongly cidal to M. leprae: 99.99% are killed in 3-7 days at 600 mg/day. MDT gives it as a supervised 600 mg monthly dose. Lepra reactions follow release of antigens from killed bacilli, so reactions are a treatment-time concern.

cards.front: How is MDT adjusted for relapse, TB coinfection and children?
cards.back: Relapse: repeat the same MDT (12 months MBL, 6 months PBL). Leprosy with TB: continue MDT but give rifampin daily as for TB. Children: weight-based doses (rifampin 10 mg/kg monthly, dapsone 2 mg/kg daily; clofazimine 1 mg/kg daily plus 6 mg/kg monthly).

cards.front: Why was MDT duration cut from indefinite dapsone to FDT-24 and then FDT-12?
cards.back: Dapsone alone needed 4-5 years (TT) to 8-12 years or lifelong (LL) with delayed bacteriological cure. MDT standard was 6 months for PBL and at least 2 years for MBL; fixed-duration 24 months gave similar relapse to treat-to-smear-negative, then WHO (1997) found 12 months similar over 3-5 years follow-up, so MBL MDT became 12 months.

cards.front: Essay: Leprosy control in India: NLEP and multidrug therapy

points: Control programme 1955; NLEP 1982; MDT introduced under NLEP 1982
Elimination as public health problem (below 1 per 10,000) Dec 2005, some states above
NLEP 2009 PBL vs MBL by lesions, nerves and smear
Dapsone resistance from 1964, relapse up to 20%, persisters
Rifampin + dapsone + clofazimine: covers resistance, quick non-contagiousness, relapse below 1%
MBL 12 months, PBL 6 months; monthly supervised rifampin, daily dapsone
Relapse retreated with same MDT; TB coinfection needs daily rifampin
Rifampin withheld in ENL or reversal reaction and in hepatic or renal dysfunction
Sulfone syndrome with dapsone; G6PD deficiency
Prevalence 57.6 to 0.66 per 10,000 (1981 to 2016)
2023-27 roadmap: zero infection, disease, disability and stigma

cards.front: How are lepra reactions managed?
cards.back: Non-severe ENL: clofazimine 200 mg daily controls it, probably through its anti-inflammatory action. Severe reaction: prednisolone 40-60 mg/day at once. Thalidomide 100-300 mg at bedtime is an alternative to prednisolone in ENL. Dapsone is stopped temporarily only in severe cases.

cards.front: Complete: diseases under NVBDCP
cards.text: The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme covers six diseases: {{malaria}}, {{filariasis}}, {{kala-azar}}, {{dengue}}, {{Japanese encephalitis}} and {{chikungunya}}.

cards.front: How did India's antimalaria programme evolve?
cards.back: The National Malaria Eradication Programme (NMEP, 1958) nearly eliminated malaria in the 1960s, but insecticide resistance and other factors brought it back by the mid-1970s. NMEP was renamed the National Anti-Malaria Programme and then absorbed into the wider NVBDCP. Use of artemisinin-based combination therapy has since cut falciparum cases and deaths.

cards.front: Complete: NVBDCP antimalarial drug policy (as in KDT)
cards.text: All P. falciparum cases receive {{artemisinin-based combination therapy}} (first line: artesunate plus {{sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine}}) with a single gametocidal dose of {{primaquine}} on day 2, regardless of chloroquine sensitivity; in the {{North-eastern}} states {{artemether-lumefantrine}} is used because of S/P resistance. The national drug policy makes artesunate compulsory with S/P to slow {{S/P resistance}}. Severe malaria is treated only with {{intravenous artesunate}}. Vivax malaria gets chloroquine for 3 days plus primaquine for {{14}} days.

cards.front: Which drug class does WHO name as the most effective for P. falciparum malaria?
cards.back: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT).

cards.front: Short note: National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030)

points: Eliminate malaria from the whole country by 2030
Keep malaria-free areas free and prevent reintroduction
Early diagnosis and prompt treatment
Integrated vector management: insecticides, larvicides, malathion fogging, biological control, personal protection
Community participation; environmental management
Epidemic preparedness and rapid response; partnerships
Planning, monitoring and evaluation
Districts placed in four categories by annual parasite incidence (API)

cards.front: Which malaria drug did the Indian review describe as the standard blood-stage treatment for P. vivax?
cards.back: Chloroquine (CQ).
refs: WEB EuropePMC Plasmodium vivax elimination from India may need therapeutic efficacy studies - Informed shift to artemisinin-based treatment IJID Reg 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12853776

cards.front: Why is chloroquine treatment for P. vivax under threat, according to the review?
cards.back: Emerging clinical chloroquine resistance.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Plasmodium vivax elimination from India may need therapeutic efficacy studies - Informed shift to artemisinin-based treatment IJID Reg 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12853776

cards.front: What does the review say should replace chloroquine for P. vivax control?
cards.back: An artemisinin-based combination therapy plus primaquine.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Plasmodium vivax elimination from India may need therapeutic efficacy studies - Informed shift to artemisinin-based treatment IJID Reg 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12853776

cards.front: Why do mixed infections matter for P. vivax treatment policy?
cards.back: They complicate diagnosis; the review says a unified ACT policy could simplify treatment.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Plasmodium vivax elimination from India may need therapeutic efficacy studies - Informed shift to artemisinin-based treatment IJID Reg 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12853776

cards.front: How is mixed P. falciparum and P. vivax infection treated under the national policy?
cards.back: Treat as falciparum malaria with an ACT other than artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (S/P does not act on P. vivax), and start the 14-day primaquine course for radical cure.

cards.front: How is malaria treated in pregnancy under the national policy?
cards.back: Falciparum: first trimester, 7 days of quinine + clindamycin; second and third trimesters, ACT (artesunate + S/P). Vivax: chloroquine as usual, but primaquine radical cure is postponed until after delivery.

cards.front: Describe the kala-azar programme in India.
cards.back: The Kala-azar Control Programme began in 1990 and was upgraded in 2000 to aim at elimination; it runs under NVBDCP with its own treatment guidelines and free treatment. Only confirmed cases (rapid diagnostic test or splenic aspirate) are treated. The disease is endemic in Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and eastern Uttar Pradesh.

cards.front: Outline India's programme against lymphatic filariasis.
cards.back: The National Filaria Control Programme (1955) used larval control, case and carrier treatment and complication prevention; it merged with the urban malaria scheme in 1978. The elimination strategy adds annual mass drug administration (MDA) of DEC with albendazole, or DEC with ivermectin, aiming to cover more than 80% of the population, plus home care of lymphoedema and hydrocele surgery.

cards.front: Complete: Japanese encephalitis control under NVBDCP
cards.text: Strategies are early case detection and management, {{vaccination}} of children aged {{1 to 15}} years, health education, avoiding mosquito bites, keeping {{pigs}} away from homes, and {{malathion}} spraying in affected areas.

cards.front: Which dengue vaccine does Sarkar describe, and for whom is it approved?
cards.back: A live tetravalent vaccine (Dengvaxia) against dengue serotypes 1 to 4. It is approved for people with laboratory-confirmed past dengue infection who live in endemic areas. It is not approved for people never infected, who are at higher risk of severe dengue if vaccinated.

cards.front: Short note: Kala-azar elimination: objectives and strategies

points: Reduce deaths
Reduce cases in vulnerable endemic populations
Reduce post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis to break transmission
Prevent KA-HIV and KA-TB coinfection
Diagnosis with rK39 rapid kits, then oral miltefosine
Vector control; synthetic pyrethroid against sandflies
Human resources; monitoring and evaluation; research guidelines

cards.front: Which antileishmanial drugs does NVBDCP use, and how does its miltefosine dosing differ from WHO's?
cards.back: Miltefosine is first line (orally for 28 days; supplied in India only through NVBDCP) and amphotericin B is second line because of its toxicity and need for hospital infusions; sodium stibogluconate is no longer used because of resistance in Bihar. NVBDCP gives 100 mg/day to all adults over 25 kg, whereas WHO advises 150 mg/day for adults over 50 kg. WHO gives liposomal amphotericin B its highest preference, but cost limits its use in India.

cards.front: Why does annual single-dose mass drug administration control filariasis?
cards.back: DEC is microfilaricidal. Albendazole added to DEC or ivermectin, given as one yearly dose in mass programmes, suppresses microfilaraemia across the population and so cuts transmission by mosquitoes. Children get 400 mg albendazole yearly in mass treatment.

cards.front: Compare the drug strategies of the kala-azar and filaria elimination programmes: what shapes each choice?
cards.back: Kala-azar treats individual cases (rK39 diagnosis, oral miltefosine first line, amphotericin B second line since stibogluconate failed from resistance), with vector control to remove sandflies; cost limits liposomal amphotericin. Filaria treats whole populations by yearly single-dose MDA (DEC + albendazole), because DEC lowers microfilaraemia and so mosquito transmission, though it cannot reverse established lymphatic fibrosis. One targets cases, the other the community reservoir.

cards.front: What has the National AIDS Control Programme achieved, and what is its current vision?
cards.back: HIV prevalence and deaths in India fell steadily only after 2004, when NACO began giving free combination ART; by 2015 new infections were 32% lower and AIDS deaths 54% lower than in 2007. The National Strategic Plan for HIV/AIDS and STI (2017-2024) aims at an AIDS-free India: no new infections, no AIDS deaths and no discrimination.

cards.front: When does NACO start antiretroviral therapy?
cards.back: Immediately after HIV infection is confirmed, irrespective of CD4 count, viral load or clinical stage, and continued for life. Earlier guidelines waited until CD4 fell below 350 cells/microlitre; WHO's 2016 "treat all" advice was accepted by the Government of India and is implemented by NACO.

cards.front: What is the standard NACO-aligned regimen for newly started adults in the Bengaluru dolutegravir cohort?
cards.back: TLD: tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg, lamivudine 300 mg and dolutegravir 50 mg as one once-daily fixed-dose combination.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Dolutegravir-Associated Dyslipidemia and Atherogenic Lipid Changes Among Treatment-Naive People Living With HIV: A 12-Month Prospective Cohort Study From Southern India Cureus 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13429048

cards.front: What principles shape NACO antiretroviral regimens (as in KDT)?
cards.back: Lamivudine is part of most first-line triple regimens; first line contains an NNRTI (nevirapine or efavirenz); protease inhibitors are kept for failure, and a ritonavir-boosted PI is nearly always in second line; stavudine is no longer used except in exceptional cases. On failure, change the whole regimen (lamivudine may continue), never add or switch a single drug. For pregnant women NACO (2013) uses tenofovir + lamivudine + efavirenz once daily as an FDC, with nevirapine syrup to the infant for 6 weeks.

points: Screening centres across India
Identify and screen high-risk groups
Guidelines for blood banks and blood-product makers
Safe-sex communication; reduce stigma
Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres: early detection, education, counselling, free ART
Prevention of parent-to-child transmission
Viral load suppression, rehabilitation, social protection

cards.front: What lipid changes did TLD cause at 12 months in the Bengaluru cohort?
cards.back: Rises in total cholesterol, LDL-c and triglycerides, and a fall in HDL-c, with worse atherogenic indices.

points: TLD as one once-daily fixed-dose combination
Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg, lamivudine 300 mg, dolutegravir 50 mg
Free ART through NACO
Dolutegravir-based ART scaled up since 2020
Dyslipidaemia at 12 months in the TLD-treated cohort

refs: WEB EuropePMC Dolutegravir-Associated Dyslipidemia and Atherogenic Lipid Changes Among Treatment-Naive People Living With HIV: A 12-Month Prospective Cohort Study From Southern India Cureus 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13429048

cards.front: Case: newly diagnosed adult HIV, CD4 high and asymptomatic. How does national policy manage ART and why?
cards.back: Start ART at once for life (treat-all, no CD4 or stage threshold) so viral load falls early and transmission drops. Use a lamivudine-containing triple regimen, now TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir once-daily FDC); keep protease inhibitors for failure. Monitor, since dolutegravir regimens raised cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides and lowered HDL in an Indian cohort. On failure change the whole regimen, never one drug.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Dolutegravir-Associated Dyslipidemia and Atherogenic Lipid Changes Among Treatment-Naive People Living With HIV: A 12-Month Prospective Cohort Study From Southern India Cureus 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13429048

cards.front: Which NRTI is an essential part of most first-line triple regimens in India?
cards.back: Lamivudine (3TC), a deoxycytidine analogue that blocks HIV reverse transcriptase. It is well tolerated and combines well with other NRTIs, so most WHO and NACO first-line triple regimens include it.

cards.front: Outline the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).
cards.back: It began as the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1978 and was renamed UIP in 1985. It gives uniform, high-quality vaccines free to all sections of society. Objectives: raise coverage in a time-bound way, improve service quality including a reliable cold chain, monitor the programme, and build self-sufficient vaccine production.

cards.front: Complete: national immunization schedule for infants (as tabulated in Katzung)
cards.text: Birth: {{BCG}}, OPV-0 and hepatitis B birth dose. 6 weeks: OPV-1, {{pentavalent}}-1, rotavirus-1, {{fractional IPV}}-1, PCV-1. 10 weeks: OPV-2, pentavalent-2, rotavirus-2. 14 weeks: OPV-3, pentavalent-3, fIPV-2, rotavirus-3, PCV-2. 9-12 months: {{measles-rubella}}-1, JE-1, PCV booster. 16-24 months: MR-2, JE-2, DPT booster-1, OPV booster. 5-6 years: DPT booster-2; 10 and 16 years: {{Td}}.

cards.front: What drug strategy does the National Diarrhoeal Disease Control Programme use?
cards.back: Launched in 1983 to cut deaths and malnutrition from childhood diarrhoea, it combines zinc with oral rehydration solution: 10 mg dispersible tablets for infants aged 2-6 months and 20 mg for children over 6 months, for 2 weeks. Prevention includes safe water, hand hygiene, food safety, sanitation and rotavirus vaccination.

cards.front: What organism causes typhoid, and how does it mainly spread?
cards.back: Salmonella Typhi; it spreads mainly through contaminated food or water.

cards.front: What does WHO say about antibiotic treatment of typhoid?
cards.back: Antibiotics can treat it, but resistance to them is widespread; in the hardest-hit regions, treatment may need more complex and costly options.

cards.front: What does WHO expect from widespread use of the typhoid conjugate vaccine?
cards.back: Fewer typhoid antibiotics needed and a slower rise in antibiotic resistance. It is given as a single injection starting at 6 months of age.

cards.front: What is the general approach to treating chronic hepatitis C under the national programme?
cards.back: Oral direct-acting antivirals in combination, never alone: sofosbuvir (NS5B polymerase inhibitor) with an NS5A inhibitor, daclatasvir or velpatasvir. These combinations act on all HCV genotypes. Usual course is 12 weeks in non-cirrhotics; cirrhotics need 24 weeks or added ribavirin (decompensated disease).

cards.front: Which drugs are first line for chronic hepatitis B, and why?
cards.back: Tenofovir disoproxil and entecavir. Both are potent oral inhibitors of HBV DNA polymerase with a low risk of resistance and good tolerability. Treatment is usually long term. Tenofovir can affect the kidney; entecavir should be taken on an empty stomach.

cards.front: What is the difference between active and passive immunisation?
cards.back: Active: the vaccine antigen makes the recipient build its own antibody and cell-mediated immunity. It is durable but needs weeks to develop. Passive: ready-made antibodies are transferred. It works at once but only briefly. Vaccines only prevent; antisera can also cure.

cards.front: How do killed, live attenuated and toxoid vaccines differ?
cards.back: Killed: inactivated whole organisms; needs a series of doses and boosters. Live attenuated: avirulent but still replicate, giving long-lasting immunity. Toxoid: detoxified exotoxin that keeps its antigenicity.

cards.front: What is a conjugate vaccine?
cards.back: A bacterial capsular polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein, such as diphtheria CRM197 or tetanus toxoid. The carrier lets infants mount a good response and gives longer protection than plain polysaccharide.

cards.front: How is the recombinant hepatitis B vaccine made and given?
cards.back: The HBV surface antigen gene is inserted into yeast; the purified antigen is adsorbed on aluminium hydroxide. Three 1 ml doses are given at 0, 1 and 6 months.

cards.front: What is a DNA vaccine?
cards.back: Synthetic DNA carrying a microbial antigen gene is injected intramuscularly or intradermally; antigen-presenting cells make the antigen. It is safe, stable, cheap and long-lasting, but limited to protein antigens. GG14 says none is licensed in the US yet.

cards.front: What is an mRNA vaccine, and what made it workable?
cards.back: mRNA is translated directly in the cytoplasm, so it skips the nuclear entry a DNA vaccine needs. Lipid nanoparticles protect and deliver it, and modified nucleosides evade innate detection. This platform was used in the SARS-CoV-2 vaccines.

cards.front: What is a recombinant vector vaccine?
cards.back: A harmless virus or bacterium carries microbial genes into host cells, so the vaccinee expresses the antigen. Poxviruses (vaccinia, MVA) and adenoviruses are examples.

cards.front: What is a vaccine adjuvant?
cards.back: A substance added to boost the size, quality and duration of immunity by stimulating innate immunity. Aluminium salts have been used for about 90 years; monophosphoryl lipid A and MF59 are licensed examples.

cards.front: Why are live vaccines unsafe in immunocompromised people?
cards.back: Limited virulence can still cause disease when host defence is impaired, as in leukaemia on cytotoxic chemotherapy, SLE, corticosteroid use or AIDS. Live vaccines are therefore contraindicated. Two live vaccines not given together should be a month apart.

cards.front: Why is IPV preferred over OPV for some people?
cards.back: OPV is the child vaccine of choice: simple, well accepted, gives intestinal immunity that also limits carriage. IPV is preferred for adult primary immunisation, where OPV-associated paralysis is commoner, and for immunocompromised persons.

cards.front: Why must allergy and deferral rules be applied before vaccination?
cards.back: Egg proteins, antibiotic traces and other culture material can cause allergy, so adrenaline 1 in 1000 should be at hand. Defer vaccination during acute (especially respiratory) infection and pregnancy. Corticosteroid or immunosuppressant therapy can stop the vaccine taking.

cards.front: How do the Vi polysaccharide and Ty21a typhoid vaccines differ in use?
cards.back: Vi polysaccharide: one dose, fewer side effects, long-lasting; no paratyphoid cover; not for under 2 years or pregnancy. Ty21a: live oral, lacks Vi, given as 3 capsules on alternate days; not for under 5 years or pregnancy.

cards.front: Why was conjugation needed for the Hib vaccine?
cards.back: Plain Hib polysaccharide is poorly immunogenic in infants. Linking it to the CRM197 carrier gives a good antibody response and protection in over 90% of recipients, as KDT reports.

cards.front: What is AEFI surveillance, and when did it start in India?
cards.back: Adverse Event Following Immunisation surveillance. It began with the launch of the Universal Immunization Programme in 1985, and national guidelines were updated in 2015.

cards.front: What does the cold chain do in the UIP?
cards.back: A series of storage and transport links keeps vaccines at the recommended temperature from manufacture to the child. The programme runs about 27,000 cold-chain points.

cards.front: Why is the OPV-0 dose given within 15 days of birth?
cards.back: OPV-0 can be given up to 15 days from birth because OPV-1 must follow at least 4 weeks later. The hepatitis B birth dose is given within 24 hours.

cards.front: Why do JE and PCV vary in the UIP across India?
cards.back: JE vaccine is given only in JE-endemic districts. PCV is not available in every state. Measles-rubella doses fall at 9-12 and 16-24 months.

cards.front: Which UIP vaccines are given to the pregnant mother and at 10 and 16 years?
cards.back: Td (tetanus and adult diphtheria toxoid): Td1 and Td2 or a booster in pregnancy, and Td at 10 and 16 years.

cards.front: Essay: Vaccination: recently developed vaccines, novel delivery and emerging strategies; India's National Immunization Schedule

points: Vaccines give active immunity; antisera and immunoglobulins give passive immunity
Vaccines are prophylactic; active immunity needs a latent period of weeks
Conjugate vaccines (Hib with CRM197; pneumococcal and meningococcal) protect infants
Recombinant HBV vaccine made in yeast: 0, 1 and 6 month schedule
Ty21a oral and Vi polysaccharide typhoid vaccines; newer oral cholera vaccines not yet in India
DNA vaccine: safe and cheap, but limited to protein antigens
mRNA vaccine: needs lipid nanoparticles and modified nucleosides; used for SARS-CoV-2
Recombinant vectors: poxviruses and adenoviruses carry microbial genes
Needle-free: oral polio vaccine (OPV)
Adjuvants: aluminium salts (about 90 years), MPL in HPV vaccine, MF59 in influenza vaccine
Therapeutic vaccines for cancer; 'negative vaccination' to dampen autoimmunity
Birth: BCG, OPV-0, hepatitis B birth dose
6, 10 and 14 weeks: OPV, pentavalent and rotavirus; PCV and fIPV at 6 and 14 weeks
9-12 months: MR-1, JE-1 (endemic districts), PCV booster; 16-24 months: MR-2, JE-2, DPT booster-1, OPV booster
5-6 years: DPT booster-2; 10 and 16 years: Td; pregnant mother: Td
AEFI surveillance since 1985; guidelines updated 2015
Live vaccines avoided in immunocompromised; defer in acute infection and pregnancy
